Exercise 9.5 — Reading the Safety Gym table
      
      
        Use the SG18 table of Section 3 and the definitions of Section 7 ($d=25$, $T_{\rm ep}=1000$). (a) State in words what $\bar M_c=0.593$ for CPO means. (b) Suppose that on some task unconstrained PPO has cost rate $\rho_c^E=0.10$ (an illustrative number). Which cost rates do the SG18 averages $\bar\rho_c$ imply for PPO-Lagrangian, TRPO-Lagrangian and CPO, and which of them satisfy "the average training episode satisfied the constraint", $\rho_cT_{\rm ep}\le d$? (c) How can an algorithm have $\bar M_c\approx0$ and yet a large $\bar\rho_c$? (d) Under Safety Gym's ranking rules, which algorithm is best? (e) Why does the omission of CPO's failure predictor matter for the comparison?
        
          Show answer
          
            (a) At the end of training, with the per-environment ratio averaged over 18 environments and 3 seeds, CPO's excess episode cost $\max(0,J_c-25)$ was 59.3% of the excess of unconstrained PPO. Zero would mean constraint satisfaction; the Lagrangian values $0.026$ and $0.018$ are small positive violations; no uncertainty interval is supplied.
            (b) Treat this as a hypothetical task whose ratios equal the reported SG18 averages; the aggregate does not determine any individual task's cost. Then $\rho_c=\bar\rho_c\,\rho_c^E$: PPO-Lagrangian $0.0245$, i.e. $24.5\le25$ per episode on average (just); TRPO-Lagrangian $0.0265$, i.e. $26.5$ (slightly above); CPO $0.0646$, i.e. $64.6$. The break-even reference would be $\rho_c^E=0.025/0.245=5/49\approx0.102$ for PPO-Lagrangian and $0.025/0.646=25/646\approx0.039$ for CPO. (Averages of ratios are not ratios of averages, so this is only an order-of-magnitude reading.)
            (c) $\bar M_c$ is measured at the end of training; $\rho_c$ integrates every cost over the whole run, including early exploration before the multiplier has grown. A Lagrangian agent that starts unsafe and becomes safe late has a small $\bar M_c$ and a large $\bar\rho_c$. This is why Safety Gym proposes the cost rate as a measure of safety regret, and why later work reports safety during learning.
            (d) The SG18 aggregate table does not determine a winner under Safety Gym's per-environment ranking. A positive mean violation means that some evaluated runs violated the limit; $0.026$ and $0.018$ do not establish feasibility for either Lagrangian method. On each environment, first compare whether the constraint is satisfied, then apply the benchmark's return and cost-rate criteria. Those individual results are needed to rank the agents. The aggregate metrics still show a tradeoff: TRPO-Lagrangian has higher return ($0.331$ vs $0.24$) and a smaller final violation than PPO-Lagrangian, but a larger cost rate ($0.265$ vs $0.245$).
            (e) Cost shaping constrains $C^+=C+\Delta\ge C$, an algebraic upper bound when the learned bonus is nonnegative, which builds in a margin against exactly the approximation errors the report blames. Without it, an active-constraint CPO step drives the estimated cost to the limit and every optimistic estimation error becomes a violation. The fair conclusion is that CPO's worst-case bound lives on the exact surrogate problem, and its practical margin lived in the shaping.

material_units.source_text:
(a) At the end of training, with the per-environment ratio averaged over 18 environments and 3 seeds, CPO's excess episode cost $\max(0,J_c-25)$ was 59.3% of the excess of unconstrained PPO. Zero would mean constraint satisfaction; the Lagrangian values $0.026$ and $0.018$ are small positive violations; no uncertainty interval is supplied.
            (b) Treat this as a hypothetical task whose ratios equal the reported SG18 averages; the aggregate does not determine any individual task's cost. Then $\rho_c=\bar\rho_c\,\rho_c^E$: PPO-Lagrangian $0.0245$, i.e. $24.5\le25$ per episode on average (just); TRPO-Lagrangian $0.0265$, i.e. $26.5$ (slightly above); CPO $0.0646$, i.e. $64.6$. The break-even reference would be $\rho_c^E=0.025/0.245=5/49\approx0.102$ for PPO-Lagrangian and $0.025/0.646=25/646\approx0.039$ for CPO. (Averages of ratios are not ratios of averages, so this is only an order-of-magnitude reading.)
            (c) $\bar M_c$ is measured at the end of training; $\rho_c$ integrates every cost over the whole run, including early exploration before the multiplier has grown. A Lagrangian agent that starts unsafe and becomes safe late has a small $\bar M_c$ and a large $\bar\rho_c$. This is why Safety Gym proposes the cost rate as a measure of safety regret, and why later work reports safety during learning.
            (d) The SG18 aggregate table does not determine a winner under Safety Gym's per-environment ranking. A positive mean violation means that some evaluated runs violated the limit; $0.026$ and $0.018$ do not establish feasibility for either Lagrangian method. On each environment, first compare whether the constraint is satisfied, then apply the benchmark's return and cost-rate criteria. Those individual results are needed to rank the agents. The aggregate metrics still show a tradeoff: TRPO-Lagrangian has higher return ($0.331$ vs $0.24$) and a smaller final violation than PPO-Lagrangian, but a larger cost rate ($0.265$ vs $0.245$).
            (e) Cost shaping constrains $C^+=C+\Delta\ge C$, an algebraic upper bound when the learned bonus is nonnegative, which builds in a margin against exactly the approximation errors the report blames. Without it, an active-constraint CPO step drives the estimated cost to the limit and every optimistic estimation error becomes a violation. The fair conclusion is that CPO's worst-case bound lives on the exact surrogate problem, and its practical margin lived in the shaping.
